newsitem.title: USA: Vermont wrestles with funding education.
newsitem.headline: Vermont wrestles with funding education.

text.p: Vermont is wrestling with how to pay for its children's education.

The state's Supreme Court ruled in February that Vermont towns can no longer use local property taxes to fund their local schools. Instead the state must restructure its system of education funding in order to provide a "substantially equal education" to every child in Vermont.
Just how and when to restructure the system is the big problem.

Unlike the other 10 states that have had their educational funding systems declared unconstitutional in the last 15 years, the state's Supreme Court did not set a deadline for the new system to be in place.
Instead, the court ruled that the funding issue be dealt with as soon as possible.

Robert Gensburg, the American Civil Liberties Union lawyer who won the suit, brought on behalf of seven-year-old girl named Amanda Brigham, threatened last week to sue the state again if substantial changes to the funding method are not in place by September - the start of the new school year.

Meanwhile, wealthy ski towns, such as Stowe and Dover, have raised defense funds to fight any change in the law that would threaten the status quo. And, the Vermont Ski Areas Association as well as other business groups are urging that a decision on overturning Vermont's tax policy be put off for at least a year.
But most legislators interpret the ruling to mean they must act this year. The legislative session in Vermont usually ends in late April.
Democrats, who control both the House and Senate as well as the governorship, are split on what kind of new funding is needed.

The more liberal House wants a state income tax, but the Senate and Gov. Howard Dean are opposed to that method. Two weeks ago, the House passed a measure that relies on local income taxes to fund education. But that measure, now before the Senate Education Committee, is unlikely to survive as key senators have opposed it.
In addition, Gov. Dean has vowed to veto any state income tax.

Dean's position on the Brigham decision has been ambiguous. While initially praising the decision, he has since expressed irritation and frustration over it. At a recent press conference, Dean was asked if he felt obligated to meet the Supreme Court's mandate.
"Who made them God?" Dean replied. The Supreme Court decision cannot be appealed.
